Henry the Seventh. A Welsh-born king who defeated Richard the Third at the Battle of Bosworth Field in fourteen-eighty-five and founded the Tudor Dynasty, ending the Wars of the Roses. His reign marked a transition from medieval to early modern English kingship, establishing centralized royal authority, reducing the power of the nobility, and laying the foundation for the Tudor golden age. Though less famous than his granddaughter Elizabeth the First or his son Henry the Eighth, Henry the Seventh was a master political operator whose shrewd governance unified a fractured realm.

Born Henry Tudor, he was a Welsh nobleman with a tenuous claim to the English throne through his mother's bloodline. He defeated Richard the Third at Bosworth Field in a decisive victory that allowed him to seize the crown and establish the Tudor line. He then married Elizabeth of York, daughter of Edward the Fourth, uniting the rival York and Lancaster houses symbolically through matrimony. This marriage and his military victory established the Tudor Dynasty, which would rule England for over a century and produce some of England's most famous monarchs.

He strengthened royal finances through careful management and avoided costly foreign adventures, building a stable treasury. He reduced the power of overmighty nobles by breaking up private armies and using the Court of Star Chamber to enforce royal justice. He sponsored explorer John Cabot's expedition to North America in fourteen-ninety-seven, establishing a claim to territory in the New World.
